bridge: Builds on C02 arrays, C03 linked structures and C01 compilation. Use your local compiler; the example avoids invalid memory access.
teaching:
A pointer stores an address. &x obtains an address; *p accesses the object at the address when p is valid. A pointer's type helps determine how dereferencing and pointer arithmetic behave. It does not prove the referenced object is still alive or within bounds.

Automatic local objects commonly live in a stack frame, while malloc allocates storage whose lifetime must be managed explicitly. These are useful implementation pictures, but object lifetime is the language-level rule that matters. Returning the address of a local variable leaves a dangling pointer after the function returns. Freeing a heap allocation ends its usable lifetime even if the old bytes remain visible.

Track ownership: who allocates, who may use an object and who must free it exactly once. A linked node contains data and a pointer to another node; draw both the node and the arrow. Distinguish pointer variable, pointed-to object and the value inside that object. A debugger can inspect these locations, but its displayed addresses vary between runs.
explanation: p and q are two variables referring to one allocation. Freeing p does not automatically reset q. Setting p to NULL alone cannot repair every alias; the program must ensure all uses stop. The diagram shows why copying a pointer does not copy its target. malloc failure is checked before dereference.
exercise: Compile and run the safe example. Draw the pointer/object diagram after allocation, after q=p and after free. Without executing invalid access, explain what would be wrong with printing *q after free or freeing q as well.
solution: The safe output is 7. After free, dereferencing q is use-after-free and freeing it again is a double-free defect. Resetting aliases in this small scope makes subsequent accidental use easier to detect but is not a general ownership system.
challenge: Draw two linked nodes holding 10 and20, with first.next pointing to second and second.next null. Describe an order for freeing both without reading an already-freed node.
challenge_solution: Save the next pointer before freeing the current node, or free the known second node before the first in this two-node case. A traversal must not dereference first.next after first has been freed. Explain allocation-failure handling and exactly-one-free ownership.
